In the long run, physics formalization may help to make classics works like Maxwell's stability Saturn rings, Berkeley Classic Purcell's Electromagnetism first edition written in CGS or Klein's 4 volume German treatise on Spinning tops and gyroscope as readily readable as any modern text??
Has that been done by mathlib for classic-yet-notationally arcane papers??
A message was moved here from #Physlib > The PhysLean café by ZhiKai Pong.
(we probably want to keep the previous thread focused on organisation and logistics of online meetings so I took the liberty to move this message into a new thread)

I think this is a nice idea, one of the goals of Physlib should be to express physics results in a consistent framework.

My personal feeling is that many physics results are developed in relative isolation and there is less emphasis on generalising things. to me it should look something like this:

We have "results" modules dedicated to stating results, and "API" modules striving for generality and reusability. the results module should contain just the main arguments and relatively simple proofs, and all the grunt work of formalisation should be handled by the API.

Although still very primitive, this is the approach I'm taking here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/tree/master/Physlib/Electromagnetism/ThreeDimension

Obviously the context is a bit different (vector formulation of Maxwell is definitely still very useful), but the design philosophy should be along a similar vein: we develop the "general" machinery (in this case, via tensors), and have a separate module for stating results (in this case the "classical" statements of Maxwell's equations).

We have "results" modules dedicated to stating results, and "API" modules striving for generality and reusability.   the results module should contain just the main arguments and relatively simple proofs, and all the grunt work of formalisation should be handled by the API.

Although still very primitive, this is the approach I'm taking here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/tree/master/Physlib/Electromagnetism/ThreeDimension

The abstraction via APIs to prove results is quite nice here! I would be very curious to understand more details on how tensorial proofs can be readily imported for proving more results, maybe in the next zoom session, if possible!
If I understand your idea correctly, we need to have layers of abstractions, each layer built upon a more complex one (like imperative programming abstracts out machine language), API and on top of that, results are two such layers. Maybe a complete research paper built on top of results can be a third layer?
